source: In the S bus, in the rush hour. A chap of about 26, felt hat with a cord instead of a ribbon, neck too long, as if someone’s been having a tug-of-war with it. People getting off. The chap in question gets annoyed with one of the men standing next to him. He accuses him of jostling him every time anyone goes past. A snivelling tone which is meant to be aggressive. When he sees a vacant seat he throws himself on to it. Two hours later, I meet him in the Cour de Rome, in front of the gare Saint-Lazare. He’s with a friend who’s saying: "You ought to get an extra button put on your overcoat." He shows him where (at the lapels) and why.

gens.text: At the bustling border checkpoint, long queues wound around barriers where belongings were divested into trays. A document was scrutinized under the officer's watchful eye as another queue awaited their turn to divest their belongings. The room buzzed with the rhythm of regulated movement; some paused for a wand sweep while others moved through the scanners undetected. In one corner, a screen displayed the schedule for flight departures and arrivals, its glow contrasting against the starkness of enforced measures. Each person who entered the checkpoint was greeted by the same formal procedure: trays, divestiture, scanning, pat-downs — an unyielding protocol governed by the imperative to maintain security without exception. As each traveler completed their check-in process, they acknowledged the impersonal professionalism that underpinned every interaction here. A few paces further down the line, another traveller received instructions for a secondary screening as part of a routine measure to ensure compliance with safety protocols. Through the labyrinthine corridors and checkpoints, everyone shared in this collective experience — an intricate dance of submission and compliance, each step meticulously choreographed by an unseen hand guiding the register of control.
